name: Americano
caffeine: Only the caffeine of its shots: a bigger cup adds water, not caffeine, so sell another shot instead.

house.ask: Not printed on the menus: ask at lineup whether there is an espresso machine, whether the bar will make an americano on request, and the price.

what: An americano is an espresso lengthened with hot water poured onto it, which breaks the crema. A double with 4 to 6 oz of water runs about one part espresso to three of water in a small cup, one to four or five in a large. The name is Italian for American coffee, and it is not a lungo.
taste: Clean and long, closer to filter coffee than espresso, the shot's body still under it and the crema broken by the pour.

steps: Pull a double, 18 to 20 g in and 36 to 40 g out, into a warmed 8 oz cup.
Pour 4 to 6 oz of hot water from the machine tap onto the shot.
Leave half an inch of headroom, with milk or cream on the side.
make.ratio: About 1:3 espresso to water, 1:4 to 1:5 large
make.dose: Double, 18 to 20 g; 4 to 6 oz water
make.temp: Brew 195 to 205F (90 to 96C); the tap runs hotter
make.time: 25 to 30 second shot, water at once

serve: In a warmed cup or mug on a saucer, milk and cream on the side. The tap on many machines runs near boiling, so it lands hotter than any milk drink; tell the guest it may need a minute.
story: The popular story credits American soldiers in Italy during the Second World War, watering espresso down towards the coffee of home. It is widely told and not firmly documented, so offer it as a story.
guest: An americano is a double espresso lengthened with hot water, clean and close to filter coffee. Milk or cream on the side?
watch: A bigger americano is not stronger; offer an extra shot instead of a bigger cup.
At the bar an Americano is also Campari, sweet vermouth and soda; ask which one the guest means.
Iced, it goes into a cold glass with plenty of ice, never a cup off the machine.

recall.prompt: How is an americano made, and what goes in it?
recall.answer: A double, 18 to 20 g in and 36 to 40 g out, with 4 to 6 oz of hot water poured onto it in a warmed 8 oz cup: clean, long, crema broken.

quiz.q: What separates an americano from a long black?
quiz.explain: Water poured onto a finished shot breaks the crema; a long black pulls the shot onto the water, keeping it whole.

quiz.q: A guest wants a large americano because it is stronger. What is true?
options: It holds only its shots' caffeine
It holds twice a small's caffeine
It is stronger built on a lungo
quiz.explain: Water after the shot lowers concentration and adds no caffeine; sell another shot instead.

quiz.q: What is the popular story behind the name americano?
options: A Campari highball renamed for coffee
American soldiers in Italy thinning espresso
A blend first roasted in New York
An Australian name for long coffee
quiz.explain: Widely told about the Second World War, but not firmly documented, so tell it as a story.

video.label: How to make an americano
video.watchFor: An espresso lengthened with hot water into a full cup. Watch how much water goes in against the shot: that ratio, not a longer pull, sets the strength, and it keeps the cup clean rather than bitter.
